tier_reason: First-party README screenshot (Apple M2 Pro) of the public harness clipper2-wasm/examples/benchmark/clipper1-vs-clipper2.html; the four rows match the record exactly. Emscripten version and browser are not stated, and the harness is asymmetric (below), so it stays C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README screenshot (Apple M2 Pro, 5,000 ops x 5,000 points): intersection 1962.1 ms (Clipper1) vs 1163.3 ms (Clipper2), shown as +40.71%; union 2434.2 vs 1817.4 ms (+25.34%); difference 2122.5 vs 1472.8 ms (+30.61%); xor 2609.0 vs 2278.4 ms (+12.67%). The percentages are time reductions relative to Clipper1, i.e. 1.69x, 1.34x, 1.44x and 1.15x faster (derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Emscripten em++ (version not stated) with -O3 -s DISABLE_EXCEPTION_CATCHING=1 --bind -s MODULARIZE=1 -s WASM_BIGINT -s ALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH=1 -DUSINGZ (clipper2-wasm/compile-wasm.sh prod); Clipper2 static library built with emcmake cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE=-O3 -DCLIPPER2_HI_PRECISION=OFF (README.dev.md). Baseline js-angusj-clipper@1.3.1 loaded from jsdelivr as shipped (its build flags not stated).
corrections.caveats: Numbers exist only as a PNG screenshot in the README (checked; the four rows match). The comparison is Clipper2 against Clipper1, both as wasm, so the gain is mostly algorithmic, not wasm versus JS or native; the category's baselines (same library native, JS equivalent) are not measured, so the entry is off-baseline. Harness asymmetry in clipper1-vs-clipper2.html and testPolyOperation.js: the Clipper1 timed loop calls clipToPaths with plain JS {x,y} arrays, so every op marshals 2 x 5,000 input points into wasm and converts the result back to JS objects, while the Clipper2 inputs are converted to native Paths64 once before timing and the output stays in a native Paths64; part of the gap is therefore JS-wasm marshalling, not clipping. Single timed run per clip type, no warm-up, Clipper1 always runs first. Browser and Emscripten version not stated. Clipper2 itself (AngusJohnson/Clipper2, C++) is a separate project and is not listed.

notes: Numbers verified against the screenshot (fetched via its signed asset URL) and the harness source read. Main shortcomings: off-baseline (Clipper1 wasm, no native or JS comparison) and an asymmetric harness that charges JS-to-wasm conversion to Clipper1 only; last commit 2026-05-18, BSL-1.0, 112 stars, npm clipper2-wasm 0.4.0.

tier_reason: First-party README tables (Node 26 and three browsers) produced by the public tinybench harness packages/bench/bench.js against @web3-storage/data-segment; all numbers match the record. Build flags are public but the README tables name only 'Apple Silicon', not a CPU model, so not A.

corrections.hardware: Apple Silicon (chip not stated for the README tables), Node 26, Chromium 153, Firefox 155, WebKit (Safari 26.6). The repo's compare/results/apple-m1-pro-darwin-arm64.md run of 2026-09-30 is on an Apple M1 Pro with node v26.10.0 and shows the same wasm rate (182.8 MiB/s at 1 GiB), so the README bench probably ran on that machine (inference, not stated).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust release profile opt-level 3, fat LTO, codegen-units 1, strip; wasm-opt -O4 --enable-bulk-memory --enable-simd --strip-producers (rs/commp/Cargo.toml); rustc 1.92.0 pinned per compare/README.md; wasm32 simd128 with a 4-message multi-buffer SHA-256 backend.
corrections.caveats: Very new (npm package created 2026-09-30), 0 stars, first-party, chip model not stated for the README tables. Harness: tinybench (100 ms, 250 iterations) hashing one constant 1 MiB buffer per iteration with create/write/digest (plus free for wasm) for every implementation; correctness is checked separately by differential tests against data-segment and Lotus vectors (compare results: 1072 checks, 0 failures). The baseline data-segment hashes through sync-multihash-sha2 (npm metadata: a node-specific sha256 export in Node, @noble/hashes in browsers); its per-call cost was not inspected and likely dominates the 11.8 MiB/s figure. The 'Fast JS (@webbuf/sha256)' row may itself run WASM SHA-256 (the README describes webbuf as an inline-base64 WASM pattern). Against the category's native baseline the wasm build is slower: on the M1 Pro, native single-thread Rust reaches 681.2 MiB/s and go-fil-commp-hashhash with GOMAXPROCS=1 343.0 MiB/s vs 182.8 MiB/s for wasm (compare/results/apple-m1-pro-darwin-arm64.md), i.e. wasm about 3.7x slower than native Rust (derived from page data). License: README and npm package say MIT, the Rust crate's Cargo.toml says MIT OR Apache-2.0, and the repo has no LICENSE file.

notes: Numbers verified on the README; harness and build profile read. Shortcomings: first-party, CPU model unstated, no LICENSE file (MIT declared in package.json/README), baseline JS internals not inspected, and wasm is about 3.7x slower than the project's own native Rust build on M1 Pro.

tier_reason: First-party bar charts (i5-4590, Chrome 102, Firefox 101, Node 16.6.4) from a public harness (originjs/WASM-benchmark packages/benchmark_base/src/benchmarkTests/*WasmTest.ts) against crypto-js; numbers are chart bars only, the Rust toolchain version is unstated and the benchmarked library version is not pinned, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README text: up to 16x faster than crypto-js. Per-algorithm results exist only as bar charts of average time for 10 loops (values read approximately from the PNGs, derived from page data): Chrome 102 SHA-3 ~103 vs ~1775 ms (~17x), SHA-512 ~288 vs ~1410 ms (~4.9x), SHA-384 ~297 vs ~1450 ms, MD5 ~245 vs ~490 ms (~2x), SHA-256 ~318 vs ~340 ms (~1.07x), AES ~275 vs ~248 ms (wasm slower); Firefox 101 SHA-512 ~452 vs ~1700 ms (~3.8x), RIPEMD160 ~422 vs ~1345 ms (~3.2x), SHA-3 ~138 vs ~555 ms (~4x), AES ~240 vs ~215 ms (slower); Node 16.6.4 SHA-512 ~300 vs ~1492 ms (~5x), SHA-3 ~118 vs ~678 ms (~5.7x), AES ~320 vs ~292 ms (slower). RSA vs jsencrypt in Chrome: about 1.8-2x (4096-bit OAEP ~115 vs ~234 ms, 2048-bit ~17 vs ~34 ms).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust via wasm-pack build --release; Cargo release profile opt-level 3, lto = true (rust/*/Cargo.toml); rustc and wasm-pack versions not stated; wasm binaries pako-deflated and base64-inlined (rust/build-rust.js).
corrections.caveats: Numbers are bar charts only; the headline 16x rests on crypto-js SHA-3 in Chrome 102 (~1775 ms there vs ~555 ms in Firefox), a Chrome-specific slowdown of the JS baseline; elsewhere SHA-3 gains are 4-6x. AES is slower than crypto-js in all three charts, and SHA-1/SHA-224/SHA-256/Rabbit/RC4 gain only about 1.05-1.15x in Chrome and Node, because the crypto-js-compatible API keeps string-to-WordArray conversion on the JS side. Harness (public in originjs/WASM-benchmark, packages/benchmark_base/src/benchmarkTests): 1 MiB random strings per item, warm-up and benchmark loop counts as parameters, same API calls for both libraries; which crypto-js-wasm version produced the 2022 charts is not stated (benchmark_base depends on ^1.1.0). Old browser and Node versions (2022). Wasm source language is Rust (wasm-pack crates in rust/). Many covered algorithms (MD5, SHA-1, DES, RC4, Rabbit) are legacy and insecure. Mulan PSL v2 is an OSI-approved permissive licence.

notes: Charts and README text checked; benchmark code located in originjs/WASM-benchmark (0 stars). Shortcomings: chart-only numbers, 16x headline from one Chrome 102 SHA-3 outlier, AES slower than crypto-js everywhere, most hashes ~1.1x, toolchain versions unstated, last commit 2024-06-25 (stale). Record's language field should read Rust compiled to WebAssembly (not a correctable field).
